title: Users Cannot Recover Cleanly From Errors
summary: This situation describes interfaces where users can detect an error but cannot confidently diagnose it, choose a safe recovery option, or return the system to a known good state. The case evidence covers simulation, workforce management, medical alarms, calibration, dermatology scanning, marine radio interaction, maritime traffic monitoring, and self-checkout queues.
keyFacts: A recovery path is the sequence of interface actions that returns a user to a known good state after an error.
Clean recovery means returning to a known good state without ambiguity, additional risk, or incomplete resolution.
A characteristic signal of clean recovery failure is escalation frequency correlating with error frequency rather than decreasing as the system matures.

In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, corrective load before redesign was 4–6 hours per detected error; after redesign it fell to approximately 20 minutes, client-measured across real deployment locations.
In the Squaremind case, a pre-redesign test with 14 patients produced 2 completions; post-redesign ecological testing produced 27 of 29 independent completions.
In the Squaremind post-redesign testing, all 12 patients who got stuck recovered and completed the scan, with recovery times from 2 to 4 minutes.
In the Kardion MCS Controller case, muted alarms were required to remain visible at reduced prominence so the recovery path remained available after acknowledgement.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Clean Recovery Failure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Users cannot recover cleanly from errors when the interface makes an error or abnormal state visible but does not provide a clear path back to a known good state. The user can see that something is wrong, but the interface does not specify what went wrong, where it happened, which recovery options are available, or whether the recovery action will safely resolve the problem.

Recovery failure is different from simple error occurrence. A system with strong error prevention still produces errors. The difference between a recoverable error and a consequential error is often the quality of the recovery path the interface provides after the error has occurred.

bodySections.heading: Domain Vocabulary for Error Recovery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A recovery path is the sequence of interface actions that returns a user to a known good state after an error.

Clean recovery means returning to a known good state without ambiguity, additional risk, or incomplete resolution.

Recovery failure is the absence of a clear path back to a valid operational state after an error is detected.

A compounding error is a secondary error that occurs when recovery is uncertain and the user takes action that worsens the original problem.

Corrective load is the time, attention, and operational resources required to execute a recovery. Recovery design directly affects corrective load.

Actionable error communication specifies what went wrong, where it happened, and what the user should do. It is the minimum communication needed to support clean recovery.

Escalation is a recovery failure signal when users reach out to support or colleagues after errors rather than recovering independently through the interface.

bodySections.heading: Operational Risk Created by Uncertain Recovery Paths
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Uncertain recovery paths multiply risk under time pressure and operational load. When users cannot identify a safe recovery route, they may attempt corrective actions that compound the original error, abandon a task in a partial state, escalate to another person, or continue in a degraded state without knowing whether the original error has been resolved.

The characteristic signal of clean recovery failure is escalation frequency correlating with error frequency rather than decreasing as the system matures. When users consistently need help after errors, the recovery design is not supporting independent resolution.

bodySections.heading: Gexcon CFD Simulation Evidence for Post-Hoc and Generic Recovery Communication
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gexcon CFD simulation case shows recovery failure caused by deferred error detection and generic post-hoc communication. In the documented industrial safety simulation software, configuration errors produced outputs that appeared valid. Users often did not know an error had occurred until they or someone else reviewed the outputs.

Before redesign, the corrective load was 4–6 hours per detected error. Users had to diagnose the original misconfiguration, identify affected outputs, and re-run the simulation. The interface did not provide a recovery path because error communication was post-hoc and generic rather than specifying what went wrong or where in the configuration the problem existed.

After redesign, corrective load fell to approximately 20 minutes. This was client-measured by Gexcon across real deployment locations. The documented mechanism was redesigned error communication that specified what went wrong, where in the configuration it occurred, and what corrective action was needed.

bodySections.heading: Triopsis Workforce Management Evidence for Abnormal States Without Structured Recovery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Triopsis workforce management case shows recovery failure when normal operational exceptions are treated as unsupported error states. Weather incidents, job delays, partial completions, and crew shortages were conditions the interface had not anticipated, so users had to construct recovery paths manually.

Before redesign, users manually reassigned jobs, found alternative crews, and handled cascading schedule effects without structured interface support. The redesign treated those abnormal states as primary workflow conditions by surfacing affected jobs, showing resolution options, and making exception handling part of the operational interface rather than an out-of-band process.

This evidence describes the before-and-after recovery-path structure. It does not provide a measured outcome.

bodySections.heading: Kardion MCS Controller Evidence for Alarm Recovery Paths After Acknowledgement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Kardion MCS Controller case shows recovery design in a regulated clinical context under IEC 62366-1. The alarm architecture required explicit design of what happens after an alarm is acknowledged, muted, or resolved.

A muted alarm that disappears removes the recovery prompt. The operator has acknowledged the alarm, but the active condition still requires response. The design requirement was that muted alarms remain visible at reduced prominence, preserving the recovery path from acknowledgement to response to confirmed resolution.

The evidence scope is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility.

bodySections.heading: Beissbarth Automotive Calibration Evidence for Measurement Recovery Paths
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Beissbarth automotive calibration case shows recovery failure in sequential measurement procedures. When a measurement is borderline or fails, the technician needs to understand what happened, whether to repeat the measurement or address another issue, and where in the sequence to resume.

Before redesign, binary pass or fail communication provided no recovery specification. Technicians had to diagnose recovery from a generic error state. After redesign, the interface used three-level measurement result communication: confirmed, borderline, and out of range. Error states specified the issue and where in the sequence recovery should resume.

bodySections.heading: Squaremind Evidence for Recovery Failure as Total Session Loss
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Squaremind dermatology scanning device case shows a severe form of recovery failure: an unrecovered error produced no outcome. The device performed a full-body skin scan requiring 3–5 minutes of patient cooperation in a sequence of specific positions. When a patient became confused and the interface provided no recovery path, the scan ended.

Before redesign, Squaremind's own test with 14 patients produced 2 completions. Of the 12 patients who did not complete, 8 got stuck within the first minute and 4 got stuck around the 3-minute mark. The pre-redesign evidence basis is client-reported background from Squaremind's own test before Creative Navy's involvement.

Creative Navy's design response treated recovery as a first-class design requirement. The Inform–Prevent–Correct framework was applied recursively across every step of the scan flow. Each possible confusion event was identified, its recovery path was designed explicitly, and the system re-engaged the guidance cycle after recovery so the patient could continue from wherever they had stopped.

Post-redesign ecological testing in London with 12 users and Paris with 17 users produced 27 of 29 independent completions. The testing was co-conducted with an independent dermatologist hired by Creative Navy. Of the 12 patients who got stuck during the flow, all 12 recovered and completed the scan. Recovery times ranged from 2 to 4 minutes, with older users tending toward the longer end. The post-redesign evidence basis is Creative Navy-recorded ecological testing across two sites.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine Evidence for Recovery Specifications That Do Not Replay Unsent Actions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Raymarine fixed-mount VHF line engagement specifies recovery behaviour for the next generation of Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF line. The new radio's name is not used. The channel encoder has a single ordinary display-context domain: turning the lower encoder requests a voice channel change only. A rejected channel request is rejected atomically: the actual channel is retained, the reason is displayed, and no retune is queued for later application.

The Raymarine interruption design stores a structured snapshot and restores it conditionally. The captured state includes the origin screen, focused item identity, list position, plot scale, uncommitted draft values, actual transaction status, and live channel. On return, each element is validated. A still-valid target is restored, an expired target produces an explicit unavailable state, and an uncommitted settings value is restored or its loss is explained.

No unsent Raymarine action is replayed. A restored call draft requires a new deliberate send. Cancelling an inadvertent distress alert is an explicit procedure rather than an undo. It is distinct from silencing an alarm and from closing a panel, includes a voice cancellation step, never displays a cancelled state after a failed cancellation, and does not present powering off the radio as a cancellation shortcut.

These Raymarine behaviours are specifications and design decisions evaluated in part on a bench mockup. They are not field results, safety outcomes, rescue outcomes, distress-response outcomes, collision outcomes, type-approval credentials, conformity credentials, or evidence that the released radio matched the specification.

bodySections.heading: Maritime Traffic Monitoring Evidence for Actions That Disclose Failure Before Commitment
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In an engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators, an audit found interaction mechanics behaving as system risks. Keyboard focus could disappear after temporary inspection, and some actions disclosed an authorisation problem only after the user had initiated them.

The designed response assigned four operator actions four meanings. Acknowledge registers receipt by an authorised actor. Assign makes a named person or role accountable. Resolve requires a governed resolution state with an attributable actor. Dismiss, where supported, hides a view item and changes nothing underneath.

A single multifunction control whose meaning changed with the selected item was rejected. Transitions expose pending, succeeded, and failed states from service acknowledgement rather than optimistic confirmation. The client is identified only by the locked descriptor, and the audit findings describe that system rather than the sector.

bodySections.heading: visioncheckout Evidence for Recovery Cost in Live Queue Operation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
At visioncheckout, a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering, recovery cost was measured in live operation on the system being replaced. When an error occurred, it took one to four minutes to resolve. During that time, three to twelve people could not check out.

The three-to-twelve figure is an observed consequence of a measured duration rather than an independently counted figure. The timings describe the system being replaced and do not measure the redesign.

In the redesigned flows, two recovery hazards were treated explicitly. Any basket change after weighing cancels the POS transaction and requires re-weighing. Rescan is destructive because it discards all state, including corrections already made. A two-step confirmation was recommended wherever corrections exist.

The visioncheckout redesign is in development. Nothing has shipped, nothing about the new designs was tested, and no outcome may be claimed for the redesign.

bodySections.heading: Design Implications for Clean Recovery
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Clean recovery requires the interface to communicate the error, the affected location or state, the available recovery options, and the point at which the user has returned to a known good state. Across the documented cases, recovery improved when the recovery path became part of the interface rather than an out-of-band diagnosis task.

The recurring design pattern is not simply clearer error wording. In the documented cases, recovery design included persistent alarm visibility, three-level measurement states, recursive patient guidance, conditional restoration of interrupted work, explicit action semantics, destructive-action confirmation, and abnormal-state workflows that were treated as normal operational conditions.

bodySections.heading: Evidence Boundaries and Limits
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Gexcon corrective-load reduction is client-measured across real deployment locations. The Squaremind pre-redesign completion data is client-reported background; the post-redesign completion and recovery data is Creative Navy-recorded ecological testing across two sites.

The Kardion evidence is formative only, and summative validation remains the manufacturer's responsibility. The Raymarine evidence is specification and partial bench-mockup evaluation, not field evidence or a safety outcome. The maritime traffic monitoring audit findings describe a specific system for a locked-descriptor client, not the whole sector. The visioncheckout timings describe the system being replaced; the redesigned flows have not shipped and were not tested.

No engagement dates are stated here. Sequence and duration are used only where they are part of the available evidence.

strongClaims: Users cannot recover cleanly from errors when an interface exposes an error state but does not specify what went wrong, what recovery options exist, or how to return to a known good state.
Escalation frequency correlating with error frequency is a characteristic signal of clean recovery failure.

In the Gexcon CFD simulation case, corrective load fell from 4–6 hours per detected error to approximately 20 minutes after error communication specified what went wrong, where, and what corrective action was needed.
In the Triopsis workforce management case, weather incidents, job delays, partial completions, and crew shortages were redesigned as primary workflow conditions with supported recovery paths.
In the Kardion MCS Controller case, muted alarms remained visible at reduced prominence to maintain the recovery path after acknowledgement.
The Raymarine recovery behaviours are specifications and design decisions evaluated in part on a bench mockup, not field results or safety outcomes.
At visioncheckout, live operation on the system being replaced showed that an error took one to four minutes to resolve, during which three to twelve people could not check out.
